title: The link layer: Ethernet, MAC addresses and ARP
goal: By the end, you can explain how a computer finds the MAC address of a neighbour it knows only by IP address, say what a switch does with each frame, read a MAC address's two flag bits, and tell what `Destination Host Unreachable` from your own address means.
opening:
Picture a café at lunchtime. The barista calls out, "Flat white for Sam!" Everyone hears, and one person stands up. The barista knew the name on the order but not the face, so she asked the whole room. Next time, she'll remember Sam.

Your computer meets the same problem whenever it talks to a neighbour. It knows the neighbour's IP address, its number on the internet. But each chunk of data it sends across the local link, a frame, must carry the MAC address of the neighbour's network card, and nothing has told it. It's tempting to think a list of every card's address sits somewhere, perhaps in the box joining the cables. Names have an address book, after all. Nothing like that exists for cards. Your computer asks the room.

Lesson 1, What happens when you curl a URL, ended on this question. In this lesson, we'll read a MAC address, watch the box that joins a link learn where each card sits, and capture your computer's question. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: Two computers share one link: client (10.10.1.10) and peer (10.10.1.20). Client wants to send peer a packet, but it doesn't know peer's MAC address yet, and peer doesn't know client's. At least how many messages must cross the link before client's packet can leave?
options: None: the box that joins them already knows which card has 10.10.1.20
One: client asks the whole link, and peer starts accepting packets
Two: client asks the whole link, and peer answers client alone
Four: a question and an answer in each direction, so both sides learn each other
warmup.why: Client sends one question to every card on the link: who has 10.10.1.20? Peer sends its answer, its MAC address, to client alone. Peer doesn't need to ask back, because the question carried client's own IP address and MAC, and peer kept them. The first option is tempting, but the box that joins the cables (a switch) knows only MAC addresses, never IP addresses, so it can't answer for anyone. The second fails because client still has no MAC to put on the frame until an answer comes back.

sections.h: A name for every card on the link: reading a MAC address
sections.body:
Here's the MAC address of the lab box's network card in one run, as Linux prints it. (The lab box is the small Linux computer, run by Docker on your laptop, that this track's Try its use.)

```text
2e:cb:30:15:a6:0f
```

In lesson 1 of this track, What happens when you curl a URL, an address like this one said which card should take a frame, a chunk of data sent across one link. This lesson zooms into that link layer, starting with the address itself. It's six bytes, each written as two hex digits (`0` to `9` and `a` to `f`). By the end of this section, you'll be able to read two facts from its first byte. First, though, let's see the problem it solves.

On one link, every card can hear every frame. The first Ethernet, in the 1980s, was one long cable that every computer clipped onto. Wi-Fi still works that way: every laptop in range receives every frame on its channel, like everyone in the café hearing the barista. So a card must tell "this frame is for me" from "this one is for someone else". That means every card needs a name, and every frame must carry the name of the card it's for.

That name is the **MAC address** (MAC is short for media access control): 48 bits, written as six bytes. Every frame starts with the destination MAC, then the source MAC. A card compares the destination with its own address and drops frames that don't match. It does this in hardware, before the kernel, the core of the operating system, ever sees them.

A name only works if no other card on the link has it. The simplest rule is to give every card ever made a different address, and that's how it began. The IEEE, the standards body behind Ethernet, sells each maker of network cards (each vendor) a 3-byte prefix called an OUI, short for organizationally unique identifier. The maker numbers its cards with the other 3 bytes and burns the address into each card. 48 bits allow about 281 trillion addresses, so they won't run out.

That rule breaks as soon as software makes network cards. Docker creates a pretend card for every container, and so do the programs that run virtual machines, whole computers simulated in software. Nobody buys a prefix for those. So one bit of the first byte, the U/L bit (universal or local), says which kind an address is. 0 means a maker assigned it, and 1 means someone made it up. A made-up address only has to be unique on its own link, and a random number with 46 free bits almost always is. Phones and laptops make up addresses too, when "private Wi-Fi address" is switched on, so that a café's Wi-Fi can't recognise the same phone on every visit.

One more need: some frames are for everybody. ARP, later in this lesson, has to ask every card on the link a question. So the lowest bit of the first byte, the I/G bit (individual or group), marks group addresses. 0 means one card. 1 means a group. That's either a multicast address, which several cards chose to listen to, or the broadcast address `ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff`, all ones, which every card accepts.

Now read the first byte. `2e` is `0010 1110` in binary, with its 8 bits written out. The last bit, the lowest, is 0, so the address names one card. The bit before it is 1, so someone made it up. That fits: the lab box is a Docker container, and Docker picks a new random address each time it starts one. The figure reads another lab address the same way.

After the two addresses, the rest of the frame is short. Two bytes of EtherType come next, the "what's inside" field from lesson 1: `0x0800` for IPv4, `0x0806` for ARP and `0x86dd` for IPv6, the newer version of IP. Then come 46 to 1,500 bytes of payload, and a 4-byte checksum that the receiving card checks and strips off. A payload shorter than 46 bytes gets zeros added as padding. That's why lesson 1's lab cut the IP packet at its own length field, not at the end of the frame.

A name on every card solves one problem. But on a shared cable, every card still hears every frame, and only one card can send at a time. Next, we'll meet the box that fixes that.

try.title: Read your own MAC
steps: Start the lab box from the `labs` folder (`docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm box`) and run the three lines below. The first shows the network card, the second prints its MAC address, and the last prints the two flag bits of the first byte.
Type `exit`, start the box again, and run the lines again. Predict first: same MAC, or a new one? Same flag bits?
On a Mac, `ifconfig en0 | grep ether` prints the address your Wi-Fi is using. If its second hex digit is 2, 6, a or e, the U/L bit is set: it's a private, made-up address.

code.title: in the lab box
code.src:
ip -br link show eth0
mac=$(cat /sys/class/net/eth0/address); echo $mac
o=$((16#${mac:0:2})); echo "first octet $o  I/G bit: $((o & 1))  U/L bit: $(((o >> 1) & 1))"

try.expect:
From one run:

```text
eth0@if220       UP             2e:cb:30:15:a6:0f <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP>
2e:cb:30:15:a6:0f
first octet 46  I/G bit: 0  U/L bit: 1
```

(An octet is the networking word for a byte, and 46 is `2e` written in decimal.) The I/G bit is 0, so the address names one card, and the U/L bit is 1, so it was made up. After a restart the MAC is different, but the two bits are the same: Docker draws a new random, made-up address every time it starts a container.

refs.title: RFC 826: An Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol

sections.h: A switch learns where each card sits, so frames stop going everywhere
sections.body:
A shared cable has two problems, and both grow with every computer you add. Only one card can send at a time, so a hundred computers share one cable's speed. And every card receives every frame, including frames full of other people's data.

The first fix was the hub: a box with one socket per computer, which copies every signal it receives out of all its other sockets. The wiring gets tidier, but inside the box it's still one shared cable, with both problems.

A **switch** fixes both by learning. Think of a waiter in the café who notices which table each voice comes from. For every frame that comes in, the switch reads the source MAC and remembers which socket the frame arrived on. These sockets are called ports too, but they have nothing to do with the port numbers that pick a program in lesson 1. (Linux's software switch keeps each of these memories for 300 seconds by default.) When a frame arrives for a MAC it has learned, the switch sends it out of that one port only. Now two pairs of computers can talk at full speed at the same moment, and nobody else hears them.

What should the switch do with a frame for a MAC it hasn't learned yet, say just after it starts? It can't know the right port, and dropping the frame would break the network. So it does the only safe thing: it **floods** the frame out of every port except the one it came in on, exactly like a hub. When the destination answers, the switch learns its port from the answer's source MAC. From then on, frames for it go out of one port. Broadcast frames are always flooded, because they're meant for every card.

All the cards that one broadcast reaches make up a broadcast domain. On a normal network, that's exactly one IP subnet, a block of IP addresses that share the same start. (Lesson 3 of this track, IP addresses, subnets and NAT, explains them.) Routers don't pass broadcasts on. That's one reason large networks get split into subnets: with ten thousand computers in one broadcast domain, every card would spend its time on broadcasts meant for someone else.

The lab network for this lesson runs on Docker's bridge network, a software switch that Docker runs for its containers. It follows these rules exactly. The Try it shows them from the outside. You listen on a third computer, `peer`, while `client` pings `router`. (Ping is a small program that sends a test message and waits for it to come back. It's the quickest way to ask "are you there?") Peer hears client's broadcast, but none of the pings that follow, because by then the switch knows which port router is on.

Notice what a switch never reads: IP addresses. It has no idea that `ee:02:07:41:4d:8c` is 10.10.1.10. Next, we'll see how a computer closes that gap.

try.title: Watch the switch from a third computer
steps: From the `labs` folder, start the lab network: `docker compose -f env/net.yml up -d`. It's a few lab boxes joined like a small office: `client` (10.10.1.10), `peer` (10.10.1.20) and `router` (10.10.1.2) share one link called lan, and a `server` sits behind the router.

In one terminal window, listen on peer: `docker compose -f env/net.yml exec peer tcpdump -i eth0 -e -nn 'arp or icmp'`. tcpdump prints one line per frame. `-e` adds the two MAC addresses, `-nn` shows numbers instead of names, and the filter keeps only ARP and ping traffic. (Ping uses ICMP, a small protocol for test and error messages.)

In a second terminal window, run the three commands below. They empty client's memory of its neighbours' MACs, ping router twice, then ping an address nobody has. Predict first: which of these packets will peer see?
Stop tcpdump with Ctrl-C. Leave the network running for the next two Try its.

code.title: second terminal, in labs/
code.src:
docker compose -f env/net.yml exec client ip neigh flush all
docker compose -f env/net.yml exec client ping -c 2 10.10.1.2
docker compose -f env/net.yml exec client ping -c 2 10.10.1.99

try.expect:
Peer printed four lines, and not one ping:

```text
17:49:31.128876 b2:34:8a:ab:b5:24 > ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, ethertype ARP (0x0806), length 42: Request who-has 10.10.1.2 tell 10.10.1.10, length 28
17:49:32.189584 b2:34:8a:ab:b5:24 > ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, ethertype ARP (0x0806), length 42: Request who-has 10.10.1.99 tell 10.10.1.10, length 28
17:49:33.212002 b2:34:8a:ab:b5:24 > ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, ethertype ARP (0x0806), length 42: Request who-has 10.10.1.99 tell 10.10.1.10, length 28
17:49:34.236068 b2:34:8a:ab:b5:24 > ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, ethertype ARP (0x0806), length 42: Request who-has 10.10.1.99 tell 10.10.1.10, length 28
```

The broadcasts reached peer. Router's answer and all four ping packets (two out, two back) went only between client and router, so peer never saw them. The question for 10.10.1.99 repeats once a second, because nobody answers it. Your MAC addresses will differ: Docker makes up new ones each time the network starts.

sections.h: ARP: asking the whole link who owns an IP address
sections.body:
Here's the gap. Client wants to ping 10.10.1.20. Its routing table, the kernel's list of where to send each range of addresses (lesson 3 of this track), says that address is on its own link. So the frame must carry 10.10.1.20's MAC, and client knows only the IP address. How does it find the MAC?

The simplest answer is a file on every computer that lists each neighbour's IP address and MAC. It breaks the first time anything changes. A broken card gets replaced. DHCP, the service that hands out IP addresses on most networks (the café's Wi-Fi uses it), gives 10.10.1.20 to a different laptop tomorrow. Docker gives every container a new random MAC each time it starts. Nobody could keep that file correct.

What works is to ask, the way the barista does. Client broadcasts one question to every card on the link: "Who has 10.10.1.20? Tell 10.10.1.10." Every computer reads it, and only the owner of 10.10.1.20 answers: "10.10.1.20 is at `4a:9d:40:b1:a5:9e`." This is **ARP**, the Address Resolution Protocol. It was written down in 1982 in RFC 826, and it does the same job today. (RFCs are the numbered documents that define the internet's protocols.)

ARP isn't carried inside IP. It travels straight inside Ethernet frames, with EtherType `0x0806`, and a whole ARP message is 28 bytes. The first 6 bytes say which kinds of address it's about: Ethernet (type 1) and IPv4 (type `0x0800`), with lengths 6 and 4. The next 2 bytes are the operation, 1 for a question and 2 for an answer. Then come four addresses: the sender's MAC and IP, and the target's MAC and IP. In a question, the target MAC is all zeros. That empty field is the question.

Three refinements make this cheap.

The answer goes straight back to the asker's MAC, not to everyone. Only the question needs a broadcast.

The asker keeps the answer in its ARP cache, a short list of recent answers, which Linux calls the neighbour table. Without it, every packet would cost a broadcast and a round trip (a question out and its answer back) before it could leave. With it, a computer asks once and then sends straight away. The barista remembers Sam's face.

And the owner learns the asker's MAC from the question itself, because the question carries the sender's IP and MAC. Peer is about to answer client's ping, and thanks to this, it can send the answer without asking anything back. RFC 826 states the rule directly: if you're the target, add the sender to your table.

The same RFC has a second rule, for everyone else on the link. A computer that already has an entry for the sender refreshes it from any ARP message it hears, even one meant for someone else. Computers that have never met the sender ignore it, so a busy link doesn't fill every cache with strangers. The last section shows what this rule is for.

The café picture breaks on trust. A barista might notice a stranger grabbing Sam's coffee. ARP checks nothing: any card on the link can answer for any IP address, and Go deeper shows what an attacker does with that.

Step through one exchange, then capture it yourself.

stepper.title: One ARP exchange, through the switch
stepper.intro: Client pings peer, and nobody on the link knows anybody yet. Watch the switch's table, each computer's ARP cache and the frame on the wire.

frames.say: Some 15 to 45 seconds later, the entry goes STALE: still used, but no longer trusted. If nothing confirms peer within 5 seconds of the next send, client checks with a probe, an ARP question sent to the stored MAC alone. There's no broadcast, unless the probes go unanswered and the entry fails.

try.title: Capture an ARP exchange
steps: Open a command line on client: `docker compose -f env/net.yml exec client bash`.
Run the lines below. They empty the ARP cache, listen for ARP in the background, send one ping, stop listening and show the cache.
Type `exit`, then look at peer's cache: `docker compose -f env/net.yml exec peer ip neigh show`. Predict first: does peer know client's MAC, although peer never asked for it?

code.title: on client
code.src:
ip neigh flush all
tcpdump -i eth0 -e -nn arp 2>/dev/null &
sleep 1; ping -c 1 10.10.1.20 > /dev/null; sleep 1
kill %1
ip neigh show

try.expect:
```text
17:49:49.341213 b2:34:8a:ab:b5:24 > ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, ethertype ARP (0x0806), length 42: Request who-has 10.10.1.20 tell 10.10.1.10, length 28
17:49:49.341243 b2:34:8a:ab:b5:24 > ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, ethertype ARP (0x0806), length 42: Request who-has 10.10.1.20 tell 10.10.1.10, length 28
17:49:49.341273 3a:42:9a:52:90:f5 > b2:34:8a:ab:b5:24, ethertype ARP (0x0806), length 42: Reply 10.10.1.20 is-at 3a:42:9a:52:90:f5, length 28
10.10.1.20 dev eth0 lladdr 3a:42:9a:52:90:f5 REACHABLE
```

The question (`Request`) went to `ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff`, and the answer (`Reply`) came back to client's MAC alone. You'll probably see the question twice. Docker turns on a setting called hairpin mode on its switch, so the switch also sends the broadcast back out of the port it came in on, and client's own tcpdump catches the copy. Peer saw it once. Peer's cache shows `10.10.1.10 dev eth0 lladdr b2:34:8a:ab:b5:24 DELAY` (or STALE): it learned client's MAC from the question, as RFC 826 says.

sections.h: When the answer goes out of date: expiry, probes and announcements
sections.body:
A cache brings back the file's problem. An answer was true when it arrived, and it can stop being true at any moment. The card gets replaced, a virtual machine moves to another physical computer, or an IP address moves to a standby machine. A cache that never forgot would keep sending frames to a card that's gone, like a barista still looking for yesterday's Sam.

The plain fix is to throw answers away after a while and ask again. Linux does that, with one saving. It keeps an entry REACHABLE, meaning trusted, for a random 15 to 45 seconds after it was last confirmed. (The setting `base_reachable_time_ms` is 30,000, and the kernel picks a time between half and one and a half times that.) Then the entry turns STALE: still used, but no longer trusted. The next time the kernel sends to a STALE neighbour, the entry moves to DELAY. If nothing has confirmed the neighbour after 5 seconds, the entry moves to PROBE, and the kernel sends an ARP question straight to the stored MAC, not to everyone. The old answer is probably still right, and asking one card is cheaper than asking all of them. Traffic that proves the neighbour is alive counts as confirmation too, such as TCP's acknowledgments of data you sent. So a busy connection rarely needs ARP at all.

Up to 45 seconds plus probes is fine for a replaced laptop. It's far too slow for a failover, when a standby machine takes over from one that failed. Some important machines, such as a database (a program that stores data and answers questions about it), have a standby twin. The address everyone uses can move to the twin when the first machine fails. Such a moving address is called a floating IP. When it moves, the new owner doesn't wait to be asked. It broadcasts an ARP message about its own address: "10.10.1.50 is at my MAC." RFC 5227 calls this an ARP announcement, and most people say gratuitous ARP. Every computer that was talking to the old machine has an entry for 10.10.1.50. So, by RFC 826's refresh rule, each of them switches to the new MAC at once. Keepalived, a common Linux program that moves floating IPs, sends exactly this.

When nobody answers ARP at all, ping shows it like this:

```text
PING 10.10.1.99 (10.10.1.99) 56(84) bytes of data.
From 10.10.1.10 icmp_seq=1 Destination Host Unreachable
```

Read the `From` address. It's client's own, so no other computer said anything. Client's kernel broadcast three ARP questions a second apart, heard nothing, marked the entry FAILED and dropped the packet. For a destination on your own link, that means the computer is off, on another network, or using a different address than you think.

**Unreachable from your own address means nobody answered ARP. Check the address and the link first.**

The link has one more limit you'll meet: frame size. Ethernet carries at most 1,500 bytes of payload per frame, the MTU from lesson 1. A ping with 1,472 bytes of data fills one frame exactly, with 8 bytes of ICMP header and 20 of IP header. (ICMP is the small protocol for test and error messages that ping uses.) Ask for 1,473 bytes with the Don't Fragment flag set, which forbids splitting the packet into smaller pieces, and Linux refuses before anything is sent: `ping: local error: message too long, mtu=1500`. Lesson 4 of this track, Routing, ICMP and traceroute, shows what happens when a router in the middle has a smaller MTU.

try.title: Watch entries age and fail
steps: Open a command line on client again and run the lines below. The `sleep 50` waits 50 seconds, so the entry has time to go stale.
Look at the ping to 10.10.1.99: whose address is in `From`?
In the last two pings, `-s` sets the bytes of data and `-M do` sets the Don't Fragment flag. Predict which one fails, and whether the error comes from peer or from client itself.

On a Mac, `arp -an` lists the cache, one line per neighbour, without Linux's state names. There, ping's Don't Fragment flag is `-D`: `ping -D -s 1472 -c 1 <your gateway>` gets an answer, and with `-s 1473` no answer comes back.
When you're done, stop the network from the `labs` folder: `docker compose -f env/net.yml down`.

code.title: on client
code.src:
ip neigh show; sleep 50; ip neigh show
ping -c 3 10.10.1.99
ip neigh show 10.10.1.99
ping -M do -s 1472 -c 1 10.10.1.20
ping -M do -s 1473 -c 1 10.10.1.20

try.expect:
From one run (ping's summary lines trimmed):

```text
10.10.1.20 dev eth0 lladdr 3a:42:9a:52:90:f5 REACHABLE
10.10.1.20 dev eth0 lladdr 3a:42:9a:52:90:f5 STALE

PING 10.10.1.99 (10.10.1.99) 56(84) bytes of data.
From 10.10.1.10 icmp_seq=1 Destination Host Unreachable
From 10.10.1.10 icmp_seq=2 Destination Host Unreachable
From 10.10.1.10 icmp_seq=3 Destination Host Unreachable

--- 10.10.1.99 ping statistics ---
3 packets transmitted, 0 received, +3 errors, 100% packet loss, time 2076ms
10.10.1.99 dev eth0 FAILED

PING 10.10.1.20 (10.10.1.20) 1472(1500) bytes of data.
1480 bytes from 10.10.1.20: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=0.039 ms

PING 10.10.1.20 (10.10.1.20) 1473(1501) bytes of data.
ping: local error: message too long, mtu=1500
```

The entry went from REACHABLE to STALE while nothing used it. The failed pings report `From 10.10.1.10`, client itself, and the entry ends up FAILED. The 1,472-byte ping fits one frame exactly. The 1,473-byte one never leaves client, because the kernel knows the link's MTU.

steps.say: A program on client can't reach another computer at 10.10.1.99. Ping gives the first clue: the errors come `From 10.10.1.10`, client's own address. So no other computer answered at all.
steps.code:
$ ping -c 3 10.10.1.99
PING 10.10.1.99 (10.10.1.99) 56(84) bytes of data.
From 10.10.1.10 icmp_seq=1 Destination Host Unreachable
From 10.10.1.10 icmp_seq=2 Destination Host Unreachable
From 10.10.1.10 icmp_seq=3 Destination Host Unreachable

steps.say: Ask the kernel how it would send to that address. There's no `via`, no router in the way, so it thinks 10.10.1.99 is on its own link and will ask ARP for that computer itself. Compare an address on the other network, which goes via the router.
steps.code:
$ ip route get 10.10.1.99
10.10.1.99 dev eth0 src 10.10.1.10 uid 0
    cache
$ ip route get 10.10.2.99
10.10.2.99 via 10.10.1.2 dev eth0 src 10.10.1.10 uid 0
    cache

steps.say: Look at the neighbour table's entry. FAILED means the kernel asked and nobody answered.
steps.code:
$ ip neigh show 10.10.1.99
10.10.1.99 dev eth0 FAILED

steps.say: Watch the wire to be sure: three broadcasts a second apart, and no answer. Peer, listening on the same switch, saw exactly these.
steps.code:
b2:34:8a:ab:b5:24 > ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, ethertype ARP (0x0806), length 42: Request who-has 10.10.1.99 tell 10.10.1.10, length 28
b2:34:8a:ab:b5:24 > ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, ethertype ARP (0x0806), length 42: Request who-has 10.10.1.99 tell 10.10.1.10, length 28
b2:34:8a:ab:b5:24 > ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, ethertype ARP (0x0806), length 42: Request who-has 10.10.1.99 tell 10.10.1.10, length 28

steps.say: So the problem is on the link, not in the routers and not in the program at 10.10.1.99. Either that computer is off, or it isn't on this link, or it has a different address. Check its address with `ip addr`, and which network it's attached to. If the route had shown `via 10.10.1.2`, the ARP question would have been for the router, and the same error would mean the router itself wasn't answering.

lab.title: Build an ARP cache that follows RFC 826
steps: Run the tests once from the `labs` folder with the command above. All 16 fail. Two of them decode the real question and answer from the Try it, stored in `src/test/resources/sfz/net/l02/`.
In `MacAddress.kt`, write `isBroadcast`, `isMulticast` and `isLocallyAdministered`. Each is one line that tests `bits` or `firstOctet` (octet is the networking word for a byte).
In `ArpPacket.kt`, write `decode`, the mirror image of `encode`, which is already written. Check the hardware type, the protocol type and both lengths first.
In `ArpCache.kt`, write `lookup` with its time limit, then `receive`. Follow the four numbered rules in its comment, in order: the order is the one RFC 826 gives.
Run the tests until all 16 pass. Then read the names of the tests in `ArpCacheTest`, in order. Together, they spell out RFC 826's rules for an ARP message that arrives.
hints: `firstOctet and 0x01 != 0` means `(firstOctet and 0x01) != 0`: in Kotlin, named infix functions like `and` bind tighter than `!=`.
`MacAddress.of(bytes, 8)` and `ipv4FromBytes(bytes, 14)` read the sender's addresses. The target's start at bytes 18 and 24.
In `receive`, check the table with `table[packet.senderIp]`, not with `lookup()`. An entry older than the time limit still counts as being in the table, and still gets refreshed.
The answer swaps roles. You are the sender (`myMac`, `myIp`), and the asker's MAC and IP go into the target fields.
A test fails with an entry that is exactly 30 s old? `lookup` must reject it when `clock() - updatedAt` equals the time limit, not only when it's greater.

drill.title: Write the exchange from memory
drill.prompt: Computer A (10.10.1.10, MAC `aa:..`) pings computer B (10.10.1.20, MAC `bb:..`) on the same switch. All caches are empty. Write every frame until the first ping leaves: its Ethernet destination, its ARP fields, and what each computer's cache holds after it. Then check the answer.

answer.src:
1. aa:.. > ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff   ARP request: who-has 10.10.1.20 tell 10.10.1.10
   ARP fields: sender aa:.. / 10.10.1.10, target 00:00:00:00:00:00 / 10.10.1.20
   switch: learns aa:.. is on A's port, floods the frame to every other port
   A: empty, packet waiting    B: 10.10.1.10 at aa:.. (learned from the request)
   other hosts: ignore it, unless they already had an entry for 10.10.1.10

2. bb:.. > aa:..   ARP reply: 10.10.1.20 is-at bb:..
   ARP fields: sender bb:.. / 10.10.1.20, target aa:.. / 10.10.1.10
   switch: learns bb:.., sends the frame to A's port only
   A: 10.10.1.20 at bb:.. REACHABLE

3. aa:.. > bb:..   IPv4 10.10.1.10 > 10.10.1.20 ICMP echo request (no more ARP)

recap: A MAC address is 48 bits that name one card on one link. The lowest bit of the first byte marks group addresses (broadcast and multicast), and the bit next to it marks made-up addresses, like Docker's.
A switch learns which port each source MAC sits behind, sends frames for a known MAC out of that one port, and floods broadcasts and unknown MACs everywhere. It never reads IP addresses.

ARP closes that gap: a broadcast question, "who has this IP address?", and an answer sent to the asker alone. The target learns the asker from the question, and computers that know the sender refresh their entry from anything it sends.
Linux's ARP entries go REACHABLE, STALE, DELAY, PROBE, and FAILED when nobody answers. Forgetting is on purpose, so a replaced card gets found again, and a gratuitous ARP moves a floating IP at once.
`Destination Host Unreachable` from your own address, for a computer on your own link, means ARP got no answer. And 1,472 bytes of ping data plus 28 bytes of headers fill one 1,500-byte frame.

The limit: ARP believes any answer, and it reaches only one link. For a computer on another network, your computer asks ARP for the router's MAC instead, and deciding which case applies is the next lesson's job.
closing:
We started with a barista calling a name to the whole café. Your computer does the same each time it meets a new neighbour: it asks the link, keeps the answer for a while, and forgets it on purpose.

Look at your own computer's list now. On a Mac, run `arp -an` in Terminal, or `ip neigh` on Linux. You'll probably see your router, and maybe a printer or a phone. Ping one of them, then run the command again to see its entry come back fresh.

Next, we'll look inside the IP address itself. Before your computer asks the link for a MAC, it must decide whether the destination is on its own link at all. How does it decide?

quiz.q: Which of these MAC addresses was given to one network card by the company that made it?
options: `ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff`
quiz.why: `f4` is `1111 0100` in binary. The lowest bit is 0 (one card), and the next bit is 0 (assigned by a maker, so the first three bytes are the maker's OUI). `02:42:...` has the made-up bit set; it's the pattern older Docker versions used. `01:00:5e:...` is a multicast address and `ff:...` is the broadcast address, and both are group addresses.

quiz.q: A switch has just restarted, so it has learned nothing. Computer A sends a frame to computer B's MAC. What does the switch do?
options: Floods it out of every port except A's, and learns which port A is on
Drops it until B sends something
Sends an ARP request to find B
Sends it back to A with an error
quiz.why: A switch floods a frame for a MAC it hasn't learned, the same as a broadcast. It learns from source addresses, so this frame teaches it A's port, and B's answer will teach it B's. A plain switch never sends ARP. ARP is for computers that need a MAC for an IP address, and the switch never looks at IP addresses.

quiz.q: A database's floating IP, 10.10.1.50, the address that moves to a standby machine when the first one fails, moves from machine X to machine Y. Y broadcasts a gratuitous ARP. Which computers update their ARP cache?
options: Every computer on the link adds an entry for 10.10.1.50
Only the computers that already had an entry for 10.10.1.50
None: caches only change when their entries expire
Only the router, the default gateway
quiz.why: RFC 826 refreshes an existing entry from any ARP message the sender sends, but adds a new entry only for a message aimed at you. The computers that were talking to X had entries, so they switch to Y at once. Computers that never talked to 10.10.1.50 don't need an entry, so they don't get one.

quiz.q: On client (10.10.1.10), `ping 10.10.1.77` prints `From 10.10.1.10 icmp_seq=1 Destination Host Unreachable`. 10.10.1.77 is on client's own link. What happened?
options: 10.10.1.77 is up, but it's set up to refuse pings
The router has no way to reach 10.10.1.77
DNS could not look up 10.10.1.77
Client asked ARP for 10.10.1.77's MAC, and nobody answered
quiz.why: The `From` address is client's own, so the error never left the machine. 10.10.1.77 is on client's own link, so client asks ARP for it directly, and after three unanswered questions the kernel reports the computer unreachable. A computer that refuses pings would answer from 10.10.1.77, or stay silent, and a router's error would come from the router's address. DNS plays no part, because there's no name to look up.

quiz.q: From lesson 1: a kernel receives a frame whose EtherType is `0x0806`. Which code gets the payload?
options: The IPv4 code, which then passes it to TCP
The ARP code, which reads a 28-byte question or answer
The program listening on port 806
Nobody: the switch removes such frames
quiz.why: The EtherType says what's inside the frame: `0x0800` is IPv4, `0x0806` is ARP and `0x86dd` is IPv6. ARP isn't carried inside IP, so there's no IP header and no port. It's the same follow-the-field delivery you traced down and up the layers in lesson 1.

flashcards.front: Which bit of a MAC address marks broadcast and multicast?
flashcards.back: The I/G bit, the lowest bit of the first byte. `01:00:5e:...` and `ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff` have it set.

flashcards.front: How do you spot a made-up MAC address?
flashcards.back: The U/L bit, the second-lowest bit of the first byte, is 1. For an address that names one card, the second hex digit is then 2, 6, a or e.

flashcards.front: What does a switch do with a frame for a MAC it hasn't learned?
flashcards.back: Floods it out of every port except the one it came in on, the same as a broadcast.

flashcards.front: What's in the target MAC field of an ARP question?
flashcards.back: All zeros. The empty field is the question.

flashcards.front: Why doesn't the ARP target ask its own question back?
flashcards.back: The question carries the asker's IP address and MAC, and RFC 826 tells the target to keep them. So it can answer, and talk back later, straight away.

flashcards.front: `Destination Host Unreachable` comes from your own IP address. What failed?
flashcards.back: ARP. Your kernel asked three times for the next machine's MAC and got no answer.

flashcards.front: Why does `ping -M do -s 1472` fit in one Ethernet frame?
flashcards.back: 1,472 bytes of data + 8 of ICMP header + 20 of IP header = 1,500, the Ethernet MTU.

terms.plain: The 48-bit address of a network card, meaningful on one link only.
A box that joins the cards of one link and sends each frame only where its destination MAC sits.
All the computers one broadcast frame reaches; usually one IP subnet.
The protocol a computer uses to ask its link which card owns an IPv4 address.
Linux's name for the ARP cache, its list of recent answers; `ip neigh` shows it.
An ARP message a computer sends about its own address, so others update their caches.
The first three bytes of a maker-assigned MAC address: the maker's ID.

explain_back.prompt: A friend who's learning to program asks how the very first message from their program to a new computer on the same link gets the right MAC address, and why that first message is sometimes slower than the rest. Explain it.
explain_back.answer: The kernel needs the other computer's MAC for the Ethernet header, and the switch can't help, because it knows only MAC addresses, not IP addresses. So the kernel holds the packet and broadcasts an ARP question: who has 10.10.1.20? Tell 10.10.1.10. Every computer on the link gets it, and only the owner of 10.10.1.20 answers, sending its MAC straight back to ours. The owner also keeps our MAC from the question, so it can reply without asking. Our kernel stores the answer and sends the packet it was holding. That question and answer add a round trip on the link, usually far under a millisecond, but if the question is lost, the kernel waits a second before it asks again. Later packets use the stored answer until it goes stale, and then the kernel checks with a probe sent to that card alone, not another broadcast.

deeper.body:
**ARP spoofing.** ARP checks nothing. Any card on the link can send an answer claiming to be the gateway, and by RFC 826's refresh rule, every computer that already knows the gateway will believe it and start sending its traffic to the liar. That's ARP spoofing, the classic way to sit in the middle of a local network. Switches can defend against it: a feature called Dynamic ARP Inspection checks answers against the addresses that DHCP handed out. The layers above can defend too. With TLS, the encryption from lesson 1, a machine in the middle sees only scrambled bytes. It's one more reason companies encrypt traffic even inside their own buildings.

**VLANs.** A VLAN, a virtual LAN (local area network, the network inside one building), splits one physical switch into several separate links, each its own broadcast domain. The switch adds a 4-byte tag, defined by the standard 802.1Q, after the source MAC (EtherType `0x8100`). The tag carries a 12-bit VLAN number, and the switch floods only within the same VLAN. Computers usually never see the tag, because the switch adds and removes it at the edge. Each VLAN is normally one IP subnet, which is why "wrong VLAN" and "wrong subnet" produce the same ARP failure.

**IPv6 has no ARP.** It uses Neighbor Discovery, which sends its question to a multicast group worked out from the target address, so only a few cards have to look at it. `ip -6 neigh` shows the table on Linux, and `ndp -an` on a Mac. Lesson 5 of this track, IPv6 for application engineers, covers it.

**Wi-Fi looks like Ethernet to your kernel.** A Wi-Fi frame carries three or four MAC addresses, including the access point's (the box your laptop talks to over the air). But the Wi-Fi driver converts frames to Ethernet form, so your laptop's kernel, ARP and tcpdump see ordinary Ethernet on `en0`.
